title: Assistive Technologies in Action 🦾
description: Detailed tour of screen readers, magnifiers, switch devices, and how they interact with your code.

slides.title: The Assistive Tech Stack 💻
slides.content:
Assistive technologies don't work in isolation – they rely on the **accessibility tree** exposed by the browser.

* **Browser** parses HTML/CSS/JS → creates DOM → **accessibility tree**.
* **Screen reader** reads the tree aloud.
* **Braille display** receives text from the screen reader.
* **Switch** emulates keyboard/mouse via scanning.

quizData.question: What does a screen reader rely on to understand a webpage?
quizData.explanation: The browser builds an accessibility tree from the DOM, which is what assistive tech uses.

slides.title: Screen Reader Commands 🎮
slides.content:
Screen reader users navigate using a rich set of keyboard shortcuts:

* **H** jump to next heading.
* **L** jump to next list.
* **B** jump to next button.
* **F** jump to next form field.
* **?** show all shortcuts.

Proper heading hierarchy and semantic elements make this navigation possible.

slides.title: Heading Navigation
slides.content: Screen reader users often skim by headings:

quizData.question: If a page has no headings, how can a screen reader user quickly understand its structure?

options.text: They can't – headings are essential for structure

quizData.explanation: Headings provide an outline that screen readers use for rapid navigation. Without them, the page is a wall of text.

slides.title: Magnifiers & Zoom 🧐
slides.content:
Screen magnifiers enlarge a portion of the screen (like a virtual magnifying glass).

* Users see only a fraction at a time – context matters.
* Design should be fluid and not rely on horizontal scrolling.
* Keep related elements close together.

**Test your layout at 400% zoom** – everything should still work without loss of content.

slides.title: Switch Access & Scanning 🔘
slides.content:
Switch software highlights UI items one by one (auto‑scan).

* Group items logically; order must match visual order.
* Provide a skip mechanism for repetitive blocks.
* Ensure focus indicator is clear – scanning builds on it.

**Example**: A switch user may take 20 seconds to type a single word. Optimise for efficiency.

quizData.question: A switch device can only produce a single keystroke at a time.
quizData.explanation: Most switches are simple binary input devices, often emulating a keyboard key or mouse click.

slides.title: Voice Control & Dictation 🎤
slides.content:
Software like **Dragon NaturallySpeaking** or **Voice Access (Android)** maps spoken commands to actions:

* "Click search" – triggers the element with accessible name "search".
* "Scroll down" – scrolls.
* "Show numbers" – overlays numbers on clickable items; user speaks the number.

Accessible names (from labels, aria‑label) are crucial for voice control to target elements.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Try It Yourself!

* Turn on VoiceOver (Mac: Cmd+F5) and navigate your site.
* Use only the keyboard (Tab, Enter, arrows).
* Install a screen reader for a day.

Empathy is the best teacher.
